prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, which brought optical frequency standards to the 10^-18 level of uncertainty

statement.case_for: I have changed my preferred configuration from B049 to B008, and I want to say plainly why. In round 1 I called the quantum spin Hall effect the most mature condensed-matter candidate, and I still think the physics is real and the confirmation broad. But my case depended on Kane, Mele and Molenkamp forming a self-contained discovery, and the exchange has shown me that I cannot defend that. Molenkamp's HgTe experiment tested the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal, not the Kane-Mele graphene model, whose spin-orbit gap is far too small to observe. A citation naming the three would therefore join a theory credit and an experimental credit that refer to different systems, and four colleagues independently reached that point. Zhang's death does not repair it, because Bernevig and Hughes are living and the three-person cap leaves no room for them. By contrast the optical lattice clock has a stable, correct allocation: Katori's magic-wavelength lattice and first strontium lattice clock, and Ye's group taking the many-atom clock to the 10^-18 level and exposing the many-body and spin-exchange physics behind it. What I weigh most as a materials physicist is reproducibility. Several independent laboratories (Sr, Yb, Hg) have reproduced and surpassed the early results, uncertainty budgets are cross-checked in routine international comparisons, and the lattice-shift and blackbody corrections are quantitatively understood theory, which is the tie between calculation and measurement I trust. Demonstrated physics already exists in the millimetre-scale gravitational redshift across a sample and the resolved many-body effects, so I would rest the citation on those results and not on the prospective searches. The topological-insulator discovery remains deserving, and I would hope it is revisited when a defensible credit exists.
statement.case_against: I still hold two reservations about B008. First, I rank a new state of matter or a new particle above a measurement capability as a type of achievement, and no deviation from standard physics has yet been found with lattice clocks; constants, geodesy and dark-matter reach are largely prospective. I accept that the colleagues who prefer B008 are weighing capability and demonstrated precision differently, and I do not claim my ranking of categories is the committee's. Second, the credit boundary is a judgement: Lemonde, Ludlow, Sterr, the PTB, NIST and SYRTE groups and the ion-clock lineage sit outside the pair, and the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes cover foundations that every optical clock uses. I think the overlap objection is answered by the invention itself, since the magic-wavelength condition for many neutral atoms is a distinct idea, but I cannot claim every systematic was first established by Katori and Ye. If the committee judged a prize without a discovery of nature unacceptable this year, I would still regard B049 as the stronger discovery, but only if the credit were reconsidered.

responses.point: Asked whether the committee can credit the effect honestly with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp alone, or whether 2D and 3D would need separate treatment the cap does not permit.
responses.response: You asked the right question and, after reflection, my answer is no. In round 1 I argued that Kane and Mele's Z2 concept plus Molenkamp's observation made a complete core. I now think that overstated it. Molenkamp's experiment realised the BHZ proposal, and a citation that credits the Kane-Mele prediction next to the HgTe observation implies a lineage that did not happen. Splitting 2D and 3D does not fit within three people, and I withdraw my suggestion that 3D could simply be deferred, because the missing HgTe theory remains in either case. That is the main reason I moved to B008 and not a change in my view of the science.

responses.point: Argued that the citation must be worded around the quantum spin Hall effect as a concept and first observation, and that Kane-Mele's graphene mechanism was not what was observed.
responses.response: I agree with your correction and it changed my position. I had treated the trio as a clean realisation of Kane-Mele and you showed that it is not. I also take your point that you would rather lose the configuration than award it on a distorted record, and I now share that standard. Where I still differ slightly is on the 2016 overlap: I think the distinction by time-reversal symmetry is real, but I would not want to bet the case on it, and a committee unfamiliar with the field could easily read it as a repeat. We both list B008 as a fallback, and I believe we can now agree on it for the same reason, namely that the credit is cleaner, not that the topological science is weaker.

responses.point: Asked whether lattice-clock tests of constants and geodesy have yielded a discovery or only a promise, and how I view the 2005 and 2012 prizes as overlap.
responses.response: Those were my questions to you in round 1, and your answer, together with Lindroth's, persuades me in part. The millimetre-scale redshift measurement and the resolved many-body clock behaviour are results in hand, not promises, and independent laboratories have reproduced the accuracy that underlies them. I still count the searches for varying constants and dark matter as prospective and agree with Johansson and Olsson that the citation should rest on what has been demonstrated. On overlap, the comb is the readout and the 2012 prize concerns control of single quantum systems; the many-atom magic-wavelength lattice is a different invention. Separately, I would note your Hall/JILA disclosure and leave to the Chair whether it calls for recusal, but I would not want the committee's view to depend on it.

responses.point: Asked whether the SI second redefinition is better waited for, and whether Katori and Ye are a fair boundary given Lemonde, Ludlow, Sterr and the ion-clock lineage.
responses.response: On the SI second, I do not think we should wait. The redefinition is a metrology-body decision on its own timetable, and the physics prize rests on what has been shown, which no one disputes. On the boundary, I defer to your judgement on the systematics, because you can read the uncertainty budgets as I cannot. I would be glad if you could say whether lattice light shift, blackbody or density shift corrections were first established by a group outside the pair. If so, the citation wording matters more, and I would favour naming the invention and the 10^-18 development explicitly, as Kroll and Pearce suggest, so that no one else's work is implied to be covered.

responses.point: Said the conceptual weight of topological band theory is not in doubt but that the missing HgTe proposers make a prize on B049 a worry; also placed a new particle above a measurement capability.
responses.response: I agree with you on the category: a discovery about nature is the stronger type of achievement, which is why I held to B049 for so long. We now differ in that your preferred Higgs prize needs a choice of three from four, which you acknowledge you cannot settle. I find that is the same problem that moved me from B049: a trio that cannot be defended against a fourth name. Because I defer to you and Pearce on particle physics, I leave the final judgement on a three-of-four rule to you. If one can be found that all of you accept, I would regard B056 as a serious alternative in kind, though I cannot rank it from my own field.

uncertainties: Whether lattice light shift, blackbody radiation or density shift corrections were established by a group outside Katori and Ye, which would move the credit boundary; I rely on Lindroth for this.
Whether the committee accepts a measurement invention over a discovery about nature when no deviation from standard physics has been found.
Whether the overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes will be read as incremental by the wider Academy, despite the distinct magic-wavelength idea.
Whether B049 could ever be credited fairly within three names, and whether the 2016 prize makes it look like a repeat; I am not sure of either.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with any shortlisted candidate. I have no personal or institutional tie to Katori, Ye, Kane, Mele, Molenkamp or the others. Uppsala theoretical magnetism is adjacent to the condensed-matter candidates only in field. I note Kroll's disclosed ties to the Hall/JILA group and leave the question of his participation on B008 to the Chair.
